note: Expected outcome per vector. Written before the validator existed. See ../CONTRACT.md.

01-oversize.json.why: 70 kB of payload. The size check must fire before the parser sees a byte, so this must NOT be reported as E_SCHEMA for the unknown 'note' field.

02-duplicate-keys.json.why: run_id appears twice. json.load silently keeps the last one, so a validator using it without object_pairs_hook accepts an order whose identity is ambiguous — two readers can disagree about which run this is.

03-nan.json.why: NaN is not JSON. Python's json accepts it by default; the C parser in another language does not. A document two implementations read differently is not canonical.

04-trailing-data.json.why: Two documents in one file. A reader that stops at the first close brace never sees the second, which is how a smuggled second order travels.

05-root-array.json.why: An array at the root, holding one valid order. A validator that indexes into the document rather than checking its type reads element 0 and proceeds — and an array can hold a second element that nothing looks at.

06-empty.json.why: Zero bytes. Not E_SIZE: the size check has an upper bound, not a lower one, and an empty file is a parse failure.

07-deep-nesting.json.why: 40 levels of nesting against a depth limit of 8. Depth is a parser resource limit, so it is E_JSON and not E_SCHEMA — it must be enforced during parsing, before any field is examined.

08-allowed-paths.json.why: allowed_paths. Dropped in every form (ADR §14) after failing twice under two names. It must be rejected as an unknown field with no special case, and this vector exists so that a future revival is a test failure.

09-absolute-limits.json.why: A plain limits object asking for ten times the policy wall clock. This is the central structural claim of §11.2: it is rejected because 'limits' is not a field of the schema, NOT because a comparison found 600 > 60.

10-negative-reduction.json.why: A negative reduction, the only way to write a looser limit in the reduction encoding. minimum: 0 makes it unrepresentable.

11-unknown-limit-key.json.why: A reduction against a limit that does not exist in policy.json. Silently ignoring it would let an order appear to constrain something it does not.

12-invented-capability.json.why: A capability name that appears nowhere in policy.json. Invention is a schema failure; an unclaimed-but-known capability is E_CAPABILITY_UNPROVEN. Collapsing the two hides which one happened.

13-duplicate-capability.json.why: Duplicate items. Harmless alone, but a set built by counting is a set that can be gamed by repetition.

14-empty-capabilities.json.why: An order requiring nothing. Not an unconstrained run — an order that declines to say what it needs cannot be checked against what is proven.

15-run-id-traversal.json.why: run_id names a directory under the run root. Anything not a UUID is a path, and this one leaves the run root entirely.

16-short-base-sha.json.why: 39 hex characters. An abbreviated sha is ambiguous by construction, and the base commit is what the whole verification run is anchored to.

17-issue-zero.json.why: Issue 0. It is what an absent value becomes after passing through a C int, a shell arithmetic expansion, or a truthiness test, so accepting it means accepting orders whose issue reference was silently lost rather than never given.

18-intent-empty.json.why: No stated intent. The one field a human reads to judge whether the result is the right thing; empty makes ADR §3.5's 'semantic correctness remains human reading' unperformable.

19-intent-control-char.json.why: A NUL inside intent. It truncates the string in C-based readers and makes the whole file invisible to grep -I, so text after it is present but unreadable in exactly the tools a human reviews with.

20-missing-bundle.json.why: No acceptance bundle. Without one the verification run has no oracle it did not get from the builder (ADR §10).

21-bundle-no-digest.json.why: A bundle with a location but no digest — the bytes at that path could be swapped between validation and use.

22-bundle-weak-digest.json.why: An MD5 digest. Collidable, and the whole point of the digest is that the bundle cannot be substituted.

23-bundle-no-approval.json.why: No approver recorded. ADR §10 requires author and approval in the run record; unrecorded approval is indistinguishable from none.

24-wrong-schema-version.json.why: A version this validator has never seen. Accepting an unknown future version is accepting whatever it turns out to mean.

25-unproven-mem-limit.json.why: mem_limit is named in policy.json under unclaimable_capabilities: RLIMIT_AS raises ValueError on macOS, so a watchdog can detect but not prevent. §7.1 defines mem_limit as prevention. The order is well-formed; the backend cannot honour it.

26-unproven-package-network.json.why: The pip-install case. ADR §2 calls it excluded, not deferred — this is the vector that keeps it excluded.

27-unproven-disk-quota.json.why: RLIMIT_FSIZE caps one file, not total written volume. Two proven capabilities and one unproven must still refuse: the refusal is per capability, not a majority vote.

28-reduction-to-zero.json.why: Reduces the 60 s wall clock to exactly 0. Non-negative and inside the schema, yet unrunnable — every run would be killed at once, which reads in the record as a failing builder rather than an impossible order.

29-reduction-past-zero.json.why: Reduces 64 processes by 100. Well-typed, arithmetically negative.

30-bundle-authored-by-builder.json.why: The builder wrote the bundle it will be graded by. This is #103 as a single field, and everything else in the order is impeccable.

31-bundle-author-builder-substring.json.why: A human-looking author containing 'Builder'. Deliberately harsh: the check is a substring match, so this is a false positive by design. A provenance rule that a rename defeats is not a rule, and a wrongly-refused order costs one edit while a wrongly-accepted one costs the oracle.

32-bundle-inside-repo.json.why: A bundle inside the patch tree, where the patch under test can modify it. ADR §10 requires it outside; the absolute-prefix rule is what enforces it.

33-bundle-traversal.json.why: The required prefix is present and the path still leaves the bundle root. A prefix test alone passes this, which is why it is here.

01-minimal.json.why: The smallest admissible order: no reductions, policy limits apply unchanged, both required capabilities proven.

02-with-reductions.json.why: Narrower than policy on two axes. Reductions are the only way to ask for anything, and asking for less must work or the encoding is unusable.

03-all-claimed-capabilities.json.why: Every capability the backend claims, at once. If the capability check has an off-by-one or an accidental all-of vs any-of, this is where it shows.

04-intent-at-limit.json.why: Exactly 200 characters. Boundaries are where inclusive and exclusive comparisons diverge, and this one must be accepted.

05-reduction-to-one.json.why: Leaves an effective wall clock of exactly 1 second. Absurd as an order, correct as a boundary: E_LIMIT fires at zero, not at one.
